concepts.name: Sati Abolition and the Role of Ram Mohan Roy
key_dimensions: Legislative mechanism: Bengal Sati Regulation Act 1829 — who passed it and under whose governorship (Lord William Bentinck)
Roy's theological argument using Vedic texts vs. orthodox Hindu counter-petitions to Privy Council
Distinction between 'voluntary' vs 'involuntary' sati in the orthodox defence — UPSC trap on nuance
Contrast with later reforms: how Sati Abolition set a template for subsequent social legislation

concepts.name: Widow Remarriage Act 1856 and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's Campaign
key_dimensions: Vidyasagar's use of Parasara Smriti as a scriptural basis — distinguishing his method from Roy's rationalism
Legislative journey: role of Governor-General Dalhousie vs. Canning (trap: Act passed under Canning, not Dalhousie)
Opposition from orthodox Brahmo and Hindu groups; social ostracism faced by first remarried widows
Comparison with Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act's limited social impact vs. legal significance

concepts.name: Child Marriage and the Age of Consent Controversy (1891)
key_dimensions: Phulmoni Dasi case (1889) as the immediate trigger for Age of Consent Act 1891
Age raised from 10 to 12 years — UPSC trap: not 'marriage age' but 'age of consent for consummation'
Bal Gangadhar Tilak's nationalist opposition framing it as colonial interference in Hindu domesticity
Contrast with Sarda Act 1929: marriage age raised to 14 (girls) and 18 (boys) — differences in scope

concepts.name: Sarda Act (Child Marriage Restraint Act) 1929
key_dimensions: Harbilas Sarda's role and the Women's Indian Association's advocacy — who initiated it
Marriage ages stipulated: 14 for girls, 18 for boys — contrast with Age of Consent Act 1891
Criticism from nationalists (Gandhi's ambivalence) and orthodox groups — nuanced colonial-nationalist tension
Enforcement limitations and comparison with PCMA 2006 — continuity and gaps

concepts.name: Brahmo Samaj and Women's Reform: Ideological Positions
key_dimensions: Ram Mohan Roy's Brahmo Samaj (1828): focus on sati, widow remarriage, women's education — foundational phase
Keshab Chandra Sen's 'New Dispensation' — contradiction: advocated women's rights yet arranged underage daughter's marriage (Cooch Behar marriage, 1878)
Debendranath Tagore's conservative shift vs. Sen's social radicalism — internal Brahmo splits over women's issues
Brahmo Marriage Act 1872: minimum age, consent requirement — first statutory reform on marriage by a reform body

concepts.name: Arya Samaj's Approach to Women's Status
key_dimensions: Dayananda Saraswati's 'Back to Vedas' approach: women's right to Vedic education and upanayana — contrast with Brahmo rationalism
Arya Samaj's promotion of widow remarriage via shuddhi and reconversion — difference from Vidyasagar's legislative route
Establishment of Kanya Mahavidyalayas (girls' schools) — institutional legacy in Punjab
Tension between Arya Samaj's social reform and its revivalist/nationalist character — UPSC trap on reform vs. revivalism

concepts.name: Pandita Ramabai and the Critique of Hindu Patriarchy from Within
key_dimensions: Ramabai's dual identity: Hindu reformer who converted to Christianity — significance for colonial reform debate
Sharada Sadan (1889, Pune) — refuge for widows; contrast with Ramabai Mukti Mission
Her work 'The High Caste Hindu Woman' (1887): primary source analysing caste-gender intersection
Conflict with Bal Gangadhar Tilak and orthodox Maharashtra over her methods — reform vs. nationalist tension

concepts.name: Prarthana Samaj and Women's Reform in Maharashtra
key_dimensions: Founded 1867 by Atmaram Pandurang — distinguish from Brahmo Samaj (not a breakaway, but inspired by it)
R.G. Bhandarkar and M.G. Ranade's role in widow remarriage advocacy — institutional vs. individual reform
Ranade's personal contradiction: accepted arranged marriage despite widow remarriage advocacy — UPSC ethical angle
Overlap with Poona Sarvajanik Sabha on women's education — distinguishing reform bodies

concepts.name: Jyotiba Phule, Savitribai Phule, and Lower-Caste Women's Education
key_dimensions: First girls' school at Bhide Wada, Pune (1848) — distinction: first school for girls by Indians, not missionaries
Savitribai Phule as India's first female teacher — her poetry and activism as primary sources
Satyashodhak Samaj (1873): marriage reforms — no Brahmin priest, reduced dowry — connecting caste and gender reform
Contrast with upper-caste reform movements: Phule's critique that Brahmo/Prarthana reforms excluded lower-caste women

concepts.name: Periyar and Women's Rights in the Dravidian Reform Context
key_dimensions: Self-Respect Movement (1925): self-respect marriages without priests, advocating widow remarriage and divorce rights
Periyar's radical position: women's bodily autonomy, including right to contraception — ahead of contemporary reformers
Distinction from northern reform movements: explicitly anti-Brahminical and anti-Sanskrit framing
Comparison with Ambedkar's approach to women's rights — overlaps and differences in caste-gender analysis

concepts.name: B.R. Ambedkar's Legislative Efforts for Women's Rights: Hindu Code Bill
key_dimensions: Hindu Code Bill (1948–51): provisions on divorce, inheritance, monogamy, adoption — comprehensive codification attempt
Ambedkar's resignation (1951) over dilution of the bill — significance as a statement on constitutional morality
Opposition: Rajendra Prasad, Patel, and Hindu Mahasabha — mapping the conservative bloc
Eventually passed in parts (Hindu Marriage Act 1955, Hindu Succession Act 1956) — UPSC trap on what was included/excluded

concepts.name: Women's Organisations in the Nationalist Period: WIA, AIWC, NCW
key_dimensions: Women's Indian Association (1917, founded by Annie Besant, Margaret Cousins, Malathi Patwardhan) — colonial-nationalist hybrid
All India Women's Conference (1927): Maharani of Baroda's role; focus on education before suffrage — strategic choice
Distinction: AIWC vs. WIA vs. National Council of Women (1925) — overlapping mandates, different orientations
These organisations' role in advocating Sarda Act and franchise rights — connecting reform to constitutional politics

concepts.name: Devadasi System: Reform Campaigns and Legislative Response
key_dimensions: Devadasi system: religious sanction vs. social exploitation — the dual nature UPSC tests on
Muthulakshmi Reddi's campaign and Devadasi (Prevention of Dedication) Act, Madras, 1947 — first state-level prohibition
Nationalist ambivalence: some leaders viewed devadasis as preservers of classical arts (Bharatnatyam debate)
Connection to temple entry movements — Periyar, Ambedkar, and the intersectionality of caste, gender, and religion

concepts.name: Purdah System: Reforms and Regional Variations
key_dimensions: Purdah in Muslim communities vs. ghoonghat in Hindu communities — UPSC trap on conflating the two
Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain: 'Sultana's Dream' (1905) and Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School — Muslim women's reform from within
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's ambivalence on women's education — modernism with patriarchal limits
Contrast between Aligarh Movement's conservative stance on purdah vs. Brahmo Samaj's active opposition

concepts.name: Aligarh Movement and Muslim Women's Reform
key_dimensions: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's primary focus on male Muslim education — explicit exclusion of women from MAO College
Later reformers: Altaf Hussain Hali's 'Majalis-un-Nissa' (1874) advocating women's education within Islamic framework
Distinction between Deoband's conservative position and Aligarh's modernist-but-patriarchal stance on women
Begum Rokeya as a counter-narrative to Aligarh's male-centric modernism — UPSC comparison trap

concepts.name: Temple Entry Movements and Women's Participation
key_dimensions: Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–25) and Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931–32) — distinction: Vaikom about road access, Guruvayur about temple entry
Women's dual marginalization: Dalit women excluded both as Dalits and as women — intersectionality angle
Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation (1936) under Chithira Tirunal — first such royal proclamation
Gandhi's role vs. Periyar's role in temple entry — cooperation and conflict between them

concepts.name: Women's Suffrage Movement in Colonial India
key_dimensions: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919): provinces given discretion on women's franchise — Madras first to grant it (1921)
All-India franchise granted under Government of India Act 1935 — with property/literacy qualifications, not universal
Sarojini Naidu's role: London deputation (1917) demanding women's franchise — connecting Indian and British suffrage movements
Distinction: Indian suffrage movement was subsumed within nationalism, unlike the militant British suffragette movement

concepts.name: Ramakrishna Mission and Swami Vivekananda's Views on Women
key_dimensions: Vivekananda's idealization of Sita-Savitri model vs. his advocacy for women's education — inherent tension
Sister Nivedita's role: Western woman working within the Ramakrishna framework for Indian women's uplift
Contrast with Roy's rationalism: Vivekananda's approach was spiritual-nationalist, not legislative
UPSC trap: Ramakrishna Mission's social work for women was welfare-oriented, not rights-oriented — key distinction

concepts.name: Theosophical Society and Annie Besant's Contribution to Women's Issues
key_dimensions: Besant's Central Hindu College (1898, Varanasi): co-education debate and her eventual conservatism on women's roles
Co-founding of Women's Indian Association (1917) — but Besant's Home Rule focus overshadowed women's agenda
Theosophical glorification of ancient Indian womanhood: reform through revival vs. rationalist critique
UPSC trap: Besant was progressive in British context (birth control advocacy) but conservative in Indian context — contextual contradiction

concepts.name: Inheritance and Property Rights of Women: Legislative Evolution
key_dimensions: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act 1937 (Deshmukh Act): limited rights — widow's share in coparcenary, but only 'limited estate'
Hindu Succession Act 1956: expanded rights but Section 6 excluded agricultural land in many states — UPSC trap on exclusions
Contrast: Muslim Personal Law (Application of Act 1937) — codification vs. continuation of personal law
Connect to contemporary: Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 giving daughters coparcenary rights — evolution timeline
